hook.line: Someone asks who locked the café door last night. You are sure, but being sure for different reasons changes what you say: a gut feeling, a conclusion you reasoned out, or something you saw with your own eyes.
hook.es: Juraría que Vale cerró la puerta.
hook.en: I could swear Vale locked the door.

examples.en: I could swear I saw him yesterday.

examples.es: No me cabe duda de que vendrá.
examples.en: I have no doubt that he will come.
I know for a fact that he paid.

examples.es: Juraría que Vale cerró la puerta.
examples.en: I could swear Vale locked the door.

examples.es: Me consta que Vale cerró la puerta.
examples.en: I know for a fact that Vale locked the door.

examples.es: No me cabe duda de que Vale cerró la puerta.
examples.en: I have no doubt that Vale locked the door.

rule:
All three say "I'm sure", but each sells something different.

*Juraría que*: a feeling. You could be wrong, and the phrase leaves that door open.
*Me consta que*: evidence. You saw it, read it or were there.
*No me cabe duda de que*: a conclusion. You have weighed it up and no room for doubt is left.

A quick test. Could you show someone proof? *Me consta*. Only your gut? *Juraría*. Sure because it all adds up? *No me cabe duda*.

All three are followed by the plain verb.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the difference between subjective certainty (*juraría*), evidential certainty (*me consta*) and reasoned certainty (*no me cabe duda*).

yourTurn.prompt: You watched Vale lock the door. Pick and type the whole sentence: *___ que Vale cerró la puerta.* (*Juraría* or *Me consta*) I know for a fact that Vale locked the door.
yourTurn.answer: Me consta que Vale cerró la puerta.
yourTurn.why: You were there, so you have evidence: *me consta*.

yourTurn.prompt: You have a feeling but no proof. Pick and type the whole sentence: *___ que dejé las llaves aquí.* (*Juraría* or *Me consta*) I could swear I left the keys here.
yourTurn.answer: Juraría que dejé las llaves aquí.
yourTurn.why: A feeling you cannot prove is *juraría*.

yourTurn.prompt: Vale always locks up, so you work it out. Say: I have no doubt that Vale locked the door.
yourTurn.answer: No me cabe duda de que Vale cerró la puerta.
accept: No me cabe la menor duda de que Vale cerró la puerta.
yourTurn.why: A conclusion you reasoned out is *no me cabe duda de que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say, as a hunch: I could swear I saw him yesterday.
yourTurn.why: *Juraría que* is for a memory you trust but cannot prove.

yourTurn.prompt: You saw the receipt. Say: I know for a fact that he paid.
yourTurn.why: A receipt is evidence, so *me consta*.

yourTurn.prompt: You trust the man. Say: I have no doubt that he will come.
yourTurn.answer: No me cabe duda de que vendrá.
accept: No me cabe la menor duda de que vendrá.
yourTurn.why: You are sure by reasoning, not by proof, so *no me cabe duda*.

yourTurn.prompt: Weaken it: you said *Me consta que Hernando pagó.* Now you only have a hunch. Say: I could swear Hernando paid.
yourTurn.why: Swap *me consta* for *juraría* when the proof is gone.

pitfalls.wrong: Me consta que dejé las llaves en la mesa, pero no las encuentro.
pitfalls.right: Juraría que dejé las llaves en la mesa, pero no las encuentro.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Me consta* promises proof; if the keys have vanished, all you have is a hunch.
Almost. *Me consta* takes *que* directly, while *no me cabe duda* is the one with *de que*.

pitfalls.right: No me cabe duda de que vendrá.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The word *duda* is part of the phrase: no room for *doubt*.

personal: Think of something you are sure about for three different reasons: one you saw, one you worked out, one you only feel. Say each with the right phrase.
